'''David I. Kaiser''' is an American [[physicist]] and [[historian of science]]. He is Germeshausen Professor of the History of Science at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT) and a full professor in MIT's department of physics. He also served as an inaugural associate dean for MIT's cross-disciplinary program in Social and Ethical Responsibilities of Computing.<ref name=bio />

Kaiser is the author or editor of several books on the history of science, including ''Drawing Theories Apart'' (2005), ''How the Hippies Saved Physics'' (2011),<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/476278a |doi-access=free |title=Physics: Quantum outsiders |date=2011 |last1=Gusterson |first1=Hugh |journal=Nature |volume=476 |issue=7360 |pages=278–279 |bibcode=2011Natur.476..278G }}.{{paragraph break}}
[[George Johnson (writer)|George Johnson]], [https://www.nytimes.com/2011/06/19/books/review/book-review-how-the-hippies-saved-physics-by-david-kaiser.html?pagewanted=all "What Physics Owes the Counterculture"], ''The New York Times'', June 17, 2011.</ref> and ''Quantum Legacies'' (2020).<ref>Phillip Ball, [https://physicsworld.com/a/quantum-inheritance-and-the-ongoing-quest-for-meaning/ "Quantum inheritance and the ongoing quest for meaning"], ''Physics World'', 47-48, May 18, 2020.</ref> He received the Apker Award<ref>American Physical Society, [https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/apker.cfm "LeRoy Apker Award: An Undergraduate Physics Achievement Award"], accessed January 13, 2023.</ref> from the [[American Physical Society]] in 1993 and was elected a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] in 2010. His historical scholarship has been honored with the [[Pfizer Award]] (2007)<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Pfizer Award - History of Science Society |url=https://hssonline.org/page/pfizeraward |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251001122103/https://hssonline.org/page/pfizeraward |archive-date=2025-10-01 |access-date=2026-02-23 |website=hssonline.org |language=en}}</ref> and the Davis Prize (2013)<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Watson, Helen, Miles, and Audrey Davis Prize - History of Science Society |url=https://hssonline.org/page/davis |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250322195103/https://hssonline.org/page/davis |archive-date=2025-03-22 |access-date=2026-02-23 |website=hssonline.org |language=en}}</ref> from the [[History of Science Society]]. In March 2012 he was awarded the MacVicar fellowship, a prestigious MIT undergraduate teaching award.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Kirkpatrick |first=Jesse |title=4 MacVicar recipients - The Tech |url=http://tech.mit.edu/V132/N13/macvicar.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161228043317/http://tech.mit.edu/V132/N13/macvicar.html |archive-date=2016-12-28 |access-date=2026-02-23 |website=tech.mit.edu}}</ref> In 2012, he also received the Frank E. Perkins Award from MIT for excellence in mentoring graduate students.<ref>MIT School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences, [https://shass.mit.edu/news/news-2012-kaiser-receives-perkins-award-excellence-graduate-advising "David Kaiser receives Frank E. Perkins Award"] (2012).</ref>

==Education==
Kaiser received his bachelor's degree in physics at [[Dartmouth College]] in 1993. He then earned two PhDs from [[Harvard University]]. The first was in physics in 1997 for a thesis on cosmology and the second in the history of science in 2000 for a dissertation on physics education and research in the United States after [[World War II]].<ref name=bio>[http://web.mit.edu/dikaiser/www/Kaiser.cv.pdf Kaiser CV], MIT, accessed January 13, 2023; [http://web.mit.edu/dikaiser/www/DKResearch.html#Bio "Short biography"], MIT, accessed January 13, 2023.</ref>

==Research on physics==

=== Cosmic inflation ===
Kaiser's physics research mostly focuses on primordial cosmology, including topics such as [[cosmic inflation]],<ref>{{cite journal |arxiv=astro-ph/0502328 |doi=10.1126/science.1107483 |title=Inflationary Cosmology: Exploring the Universe from the Smallest to the Largest Scales |date=2005 |last1=Guth |first1=Alan H. |last2=Kaiser |first2=David I. |journal=Science |volume=307 |issue=5711 |pages=884–890 |pmid=15705842 |bibcode=2005Sci...307..884G }}</ref> post-inflation reheating,<ref>{{cite journal |arxiv=1410.3808 |doi=10.1142/S0218271815300037 |title=Nonperturbative dynamics of reheating after inflation: A review |date=2015 |last1=Amin |first1=Mustafa A. |last2=Hertzberg |first2=Mark P. |last3=Kaiser |first3=David I. |last4=Karouby |first4=Johanna |journal=International Journal of Modern Physics D |volume=24 |issue=1 |bibcode=2015IJMPD..2430003A }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |arxiv=1905.12562 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.123.171301 |title=Nonlinear Dynamics of Preheating after Multifield Inflation with Nonminimal Couplings |date=2019 |last1=Nguyen |first1=Rachel |last2=Van De Vis |first2=Jorinde |last3=Sfakianakis |first3=Evangelos I. |last4=Giblin |first4=John T. |last5=Kaiser |first5=David I. |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=123 |issue=17 |article-number=171301 |pmid=31702236 |bibcode=2019PhRvL.123q1301N }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |arxiv=2006.16182 |doi=10.21105/astro.2006.16182  |doi-access=free|title=The First Three Seconds: A Review of Possible Expansion Histories of the Early Universe |date=2021 |last1=Allahverdi |first1=Rouzbeh |last2=Amin |first2=Mustafa A. |last3=Berlin |first3=Asher |last4=Bernal |first4=Nicholas |last5=Byrnes |first5=Christian T. |last6=Delos |first6=M. Sten |last7=Erickcek |first7=Adrienne L. |last8=Escudero |first8=Miguel |last9=Figueroa |first9=Daniel G. |last10=Freese |first10=Katherine |last11=Harada |first11=Tomohiro |last12=Hooper |first12=Dan |last13=Kaiser |first13=David I. |last14=Karwal |first14=Tanvi |last15=Kohri |first15=Kazunori |last16=Krnjaci |first16=Gordan |last17=Lewicki |first17=Marek |last18=Lozanov |first18=Kaloian D. |last19=Poulin |first19=Vivian |last20=Sinha |first20=Kuver |last21=Smith |first21=Tristan L. |last22=Takahashi |first22=Tomo |last23=Tenkanen |first23=Tommi |last24=Unwin |first24=James  |last25=Vaskonen |first25=Ville |last26=Watson |first26=Scott |journal=The Open Journal of Astrophysics |volume=4 |issue=1 |page=1 |bibcode=2021OJAp....4E...1A }}</ref> and [[primordial black holes]].<ref name=":3">{{cite journal |arxiv=2205.04471 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.106.063535 |title=Primordial black holes from multifield inflation with nonminimal couplings |date=2022 |last1=Geller |first1=Sarah R. |last2=Qin |first2=Wenzer |last3=McDonough |first3=Evan |last4=Kaiser |first4=David I. |journal=Physical Review D |volume=106 |issue=6 |article-number=063535 |bibcode=2022PhRvD.106f3535G }}</ref> In particular, he and colleagues have studied a wide range of initial conditions under which inflation will begin, as well as constructing models of inflation that include features motivated by high-energy particle physics, such as multiple interacting fields with nonminimal couplings to spacetime curvature.<ref>{{Citation |last=Kaiser |first=David I. |title=Nonminimal Couplings in the Early Universe: Multifield Models of Inflation and the Latest Observations |date=2016-05-07 |arxiv=1511.09148}}</ref> 

This work includes some of the first calculations of predictions from such models for observable features such as the [[spectral index]] of primordial perturbations measured in the [[cosmic microwave background]] radiation, the first demonstration that resonant particle production during the reheating phase can persist amid an expanding universe, and the first demonstration of attractor behaviors in multifield models.<ref>David Kaiser, [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LRRZPBCnGYY&t=3s "Primordial Black Holes as Dark Matter Candidates"], Black Hole Initiative, Harvard University, December 12, 2022.</ref>  More recent work has identified distinct processes within the late stages of the reheating phase, which ultimately yield the conditions for standard [[Big Bang]] evolution: a hot plasma of [[Standard Model]] particles in thermal equilibrium.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Guth |first1=Alan H. |last2=Kaiser |first2=David I. |last3=Nomura |first3=Yasunori |date=2014 |title=Inflationary paradigm after Planck 2013 |journal=Physics Letters B |volume=733 |pages=112–119 |arxiv=1312.7619 |bibcode=2014PhLB..733..112G |doi=10.1016/j.physletb.2014.03.020}}</ref>

=== Primordial black holes ===
Some of Kaiser's research focuses on [[Primordial black hole|primordial black holes]], especially as a viable candidate for [[dark matter]]. Unlike various hypothetical particles, such as [[Weakly interacting massive particle|weakly interacting massive particles]] (WIMPs) or ultralight particles such as [[Axion|axions]], primordial black holes would not require any new particles beyond the Standard Model in order to account for the measured dark matter abundance.<ref name=":4">{{cite journal |last1=Qin |first1=Wenzer |last2=Geller |first2=Sarah R. |last3=Balaji |first3=Shyam |last4=McDonough |first4=Evan |last5=Kaiser |first5=David I. |date=2023 |title=Planck constraints and gravitational wave forecasts for primordial black hole dark matter seeded by multifield inflation |journal=Physical Review D |volume=108 |issue=4 |article-number=043508 |arxiv=2303.02168 |bibcode=2023PhRvD.108d3508Q |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.108.043508}}</ref> Kaiser also explores the possibility of identifying primordial black holes by detecting exceptionally high-energy neutrinos, emitted as part of these objects' [[Hawking radiation]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Klipfel |first=Alexandra P. |last2=Kaiser |first2=David I. |date=September 18, 2025 |title=Ultrahigh-Energy Neutrinos from Primordial Black Holes |url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/vnm4-7wdc |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=135 |issue=12 |pages=121003 |doi=10.1103/vnm4-7wdc|arxiv=2503.19227 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=O'Callaghan |first=Jonathan |date=January 23, 2026 |title=Monster Neutrino Could Be a Messenger of Ancient Black Holes |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/monster-neutrino-could-be-a-messenger-of-ancient-black-holes-20260123/ |access-date=May 11, 2026 |work=Quanta Magazine}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Overbye |first=Dennis |date=2026-03-27 |title=Did Scientists Just Detect an Exploding Black Hole? |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/27/science/astrophysics-neutrinos-black-holes.html |access-date=2026-05-19 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

Kaiser and his colleagues have studied mechanisms by which a population of primordial black holes could have formed during the very early universe in models that preserve the close fit between predictions and observations of the cosmic microwave background radiation.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" /> They have also identified a possible subpopulation of primordial black holes that would have formed with significant [[Color charge|QCD color charge]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Alonso-Monsalve |first1=Elba |last2=Kaiser |first2=David I. |date=2024 |title=Primordial Black Holes with QCD Color Charge |url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.132.231402 |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=132 |issue=23 |article-number=231402 |arxiv=2310.16877 |bibcode=2024PhRvL.132w1402A |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.132.231402 |pmid=38905659}}</ref> constituting a novel [[state of matter]]. Additionally, they have proposed a new observable test to help establish whether primordial black holes exist and contribute significantly to dark matter abundance, based on high-precision measurements of visible objects within the Solar System, such as the planet Mars.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Tran |first1=Tung X. |title=Close encounters of the primordial kind: A new observable for primordial black holes as dark matter |date=2024-09-16 |arxiv=2312.17217 |last2=Geller |first2=Sarah R. |last3=Lehmann |first3=Benjamin V. |last4=Kaiser |first4=David I.|journal=Physical Review D |volume=110 |issue=6 |article-number=063533 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.110.063533 |bibcode=2024PhRvD.110f3533T }}</ref> 

=== Experimental tests of quantum theory ===
Kaiser has also helped to design and conduct novel experimental tests of [[quantum mechanics]]. In one such test, Kaiser and colleagues demonstrated how measurements of [[Neutrino oscillation|neutrino oscillations]] could be used to test whether quantum objects really persist in [[Quantum superposition|superposition]] states—akin to [[Schrödinger's cat|Schrödinger's cat]]—between preparation and measurement. By applying the neutrino measurements to the [[Leggett–Garg inequality|Leggett-Garg inequality]], their long-baseline test showed clear evidence of quantum superpositions over a distance of 450 miles (720 km).<ref>{{Citation |last1=Formaggio |first1=J. A. |title=Violation of the Leggett-Garg Inequality in Neutrino Oscillations |date=2016-07-28 |arxiv=1602.00041 |last2=Kaiser |first2=D. I. |last3=Murskyj |first3=M. M. |last4=Weiss |first4=T. E.|journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=117 |issue=5 |article-number=050402 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.117.050402 |pmid=27517759 |bibcode=2016PhRvL.117e0402F }}</ref>

In a separate project, Kaiser and colleagues first proposed a novel protocol for experimental tests of [[Bell's theorem|Bell's inequality]] to address the so-called "freedom-of-choice" loophole.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Gallicchio |first1=Jason |title=Testing Bell's Inequality with Cosmic Photons: Closing the Setting-Independence Loophole |date=2014-02-21 |last2=Friedman |first2=Andrew S. |last3=Kaiser |first3=David I.|journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=112 |issue=11 |article-number=110405 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.112.110405 |pmid=24702336 |arxiv=1310.3288 |bibcode=2014PhRvL.112k0405G }}</ref> Working with Nobel laureate [[Anton Zeilinger]] and his group,<ref name=":5">David Kaiser, [https://nautil.us/they-probed-quantum-entanglement-while-everyone-shrugged-241212/ "They probed quantum entanglement while everyone shrugged"], ''Nautilus'', October 5, 2022.</ref> their "Cosmic Bell" experiments demonstrated [[quantum entanglement]] while using real-time astronomical measurements of cosmologically distant events to determine the types of measurements performed on each member of an entangled pair.<ref name=":5" /> These experiments placed the tightest constraints yet on certain types of alternative models to quantum theory, excluding nearly all possible exploitation of the freedom-of-choice loophole from the causal past of the experiments, extending from the Big Bang to today.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Handsteiner |first1=Johannes |last2=et al. (Cosmic Bell collaboration) |date=2017 |title=Cosmic Bell Test: Measurement Settings from Milky Way Stars |url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.118.060401 |journal=[[Physical Review Letters]] |volume=118 |issue=6 |article-number=060401 |arxiv=1611.06985 |bibcode=2017PhRvL.118f0401H |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.118.060401 |pmid=28234500}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rauch |first1=Dominik |last2=et al. (Cosmic Bell collaboration) |date=2018 |title=Cosmic Bell Test Using Random Measurement Settings from High-Redshift Quasars |url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.121.080403 |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=121 |issue=8 |article-number=080403 |arxiv=1808.05966 |bibcode=2018PhRvL.121h0403R |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.121.080403 |pmid=30192604}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Kaiser |first=David |date=2017-02-07 |title=Quantum Theory by Starlight |url=https://www.newyorker.com/tech/annals-of-technology/quantum-theory-by-starlight |access-date=2024-12-17 |magazine=The New Yorker |language=en-US |issn=0028-792X}}</ref> The Cosmic Bell experiments were featured in the PBS NOVA documentary film ''Einstein's Quantum Riddle'' (2019).<ref>{{Cite web |last=NOVA PBS |date=January 9, 2019 |title=Einstein's Quantum Riddle |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=068rdc75mHM |website=YouTube |publisher=WGBH Educational Foundation}}</ref>

== Research on the history of physics ==
Kaiser's historical research focuses on intersections among modern natural sciences, geopolitics, and the history of higher education during the Cold War. His major historical publications include:

* ''Drawing Theories Apart: The Dispersion of Feynman Diagrams in Postwar Physics'' (2005) – A study of how the American physicist [[Richard Feynman]]'s idiosyncratic approach to high-energy physics entered the mainstream. Recipient of the [[Pfizer Award]] from the History of Science Society.<ref name=":0" /> Historian of science Melinda Baldwin called it an "essential" book on the history of physics.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Baldwin |first=Melinda |date=September 15, 2016 |title=Five essential history of physics books |url=https://physicstoday.aip.org/news/five-essential-history-of-physics-books |journal=[[Physics Today]] |doi=10.1063/PT.5.3039|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Physicist [[Eugen Merzbacher]] praised it as "colorful and readable account" of the early history of [[Feynman diagram|Feynman diagrams]] that included [[Primary source|first-hand accounts]] from the people who developed [[quantum electrodynamics]] after World War II.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Merzbacher |first=Eugen |date=November 1, 2006 |title=Review: ''Drawing Theories Apart: The Dispersion of Feynman Diagrams in Postwar Physics'' |url=https://physicstoday.aip.org/reviews/drawing-theories-apart-the-dispersion-of-feynman-diagrams-in-postwar-physics |journal=[[Physics Today]] |doi=10.1063/1.2435652|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* ''How the Hippies Saved Physics: Science, Counterculture, and the Quantum Revival'' (2011) – An exploration of how [[Counterculture of the 1960s|countercultural]] figures became some of the earliest physicists to focus on [[Bell's theorem|Bell's theorem]] and quantum entanglement during the 1960s and 1970s. This book received the Davis Prize from the History of Science Society<ref name=":1" /> and was named "Book of the Year" by ''Physics World'' magazine in 2012.<ref>{{Cite news |date=December 18, 2012 |title=Physics World's 2012 Book of the Year |url=https://physicsworld.com/a/physics-worlds-2012-book-of-the-year/ |access-date=February 23, 2026 |work=Physics World}}</ref>
* ''Quantum Legacies: Dispatches from an Uncertain World'' (2020) – An [[anthology]] of essays on the history and sociology of the development of quantum mechanics, covering funding for research as well as trends in research, teaching, and publishing.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Ball |first=Phillip |date=May 18, 2020 |title=Quantum inheritance and the ongoing quest for meaning |url=https://physicsworld.com/a/quantum-inheritance-and-the-ongoing-quest-for-meaning/ |access-date=February 23, 2026 |work=[[Physics World]]|author-link=Philip Ball}}</ref> These essays may be read in arbitrary order, and may be perused by both physicists and laypersons alike. It features many statistics and metaphors.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Reed |first=Cameron |date=January 1, 2021 |title=Review: ''Quantum Legacies: Dispatches from an Uncertain World'' |url=https://pubs.aip.org/aapt/ajp/article/89/1/123/1045735/Quantum-Legacies-Dispatches-from-an-Uncertain |journal=[[American Journal of Physics]] |volume=89 |issue=1 |pages=123-4 |doi=10.1119/10.0002262}}</ref>

His MIT course on "Einstein, Oppenheimer, Feynman: Physics in the Twentieth Century" is available via [[MIT OpenCourseWare]].<ref>{{cite web | title=Einstein, Oppenheimer, Feynman: Physics in the 20th Century | website=MIT OpenCourseWare | url=https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/sts-042-einstein-oppenheimer-feynman-physics-in-the-20th-century-fall-2020/ | access-date=September 12, 2025}}</ref> In addition
